newsitem.title: USA: Dow hits another high, bonds rise.
newsitem.headline: Dow hits another high, bonds rise.

text.p: Stocks jumped to record highs yet again Wednesday on strength in blue-chip issues such as General Motors Corp., Caterpillar Inc. and Boeing Co.
Bonds rose for a second day in a row on solid demand for the Treasury's auction of five-year notes. Oil prices fell and the dollar ended mixed.
The 30-share Dow average rose 32.42 points to 6,430.02, beating Tuesday's record of 6,397.60. It was the Dow's 10th new high so far this month and 41st this year.
In the broader market, advancing issues led declines 1,350 to 1,068 on active volume of 489 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
"There's no question it's frothy but this is sustainable as long as bond yields stay to the market's advantage," said Joseph Battipaglia, chief investment officer at Gruntal & Co.

In the bond market, the 30-year Treasury added 11/32, or $3.44 on a $1,000 bond, lowering its yield to 6.41 percent from 6.44 percent on Tuesday. Bonds got a boost from the successful auction of $12.5 billion of five-year U.S. notes, traders said.

"If you made a model of what drives the stock market you'd have to say none of the variables is changing except bond yields," Battipaglia said. Bond yields below 7 percent often drive investors to plough money into stocks.

While several broader market gauges again hit records -- among them the NYSE composite index and the Standard & Poor's index of 500 stocks -- the Dow again outperformed other market measures, extending a trend that has raised yellow warning flags on Wall Street.
Among them was Prime Charter Ltd.'s Chief Investment Strategist Scott Bleier, who reduced the amount of stocks and bonds in his firm's asset allocation model, citing the recent run-up in prices.
"We feel that the activity in the first-tier, largest capitalised names has reached frenetic levels," he said.
Despite mounting caution, investors were still buying any blue chip stock that appeared poised to outperform other issues, such as Caterpillar.

"There's so much money still waiting to get in on any reason," said Robert Froehlich, chief investment strategist Van Kampen American Capital. "Any move from a hold to a buy has the potential to move a stock like this."
In currency markets, the dollar fell against European currencies after a jump in the U.S. trade deficit prompted worries that the strong dollar was hurting exports.
The dollar stood at 1.4965 German marks late in New York, down from 1.5055 marks late on Tuesday. But it rose to 111.55 Japanese yen from 111.65 yen.

Wheat prices jumped, boosted by tight stockpiles and farmers' reluctance to sell their crops following a prolonged slide in prices. December wheat rose 15-1/2 cents to $4.13-1/4 a bushel at the Chicago Board of Trade, where prices for nearby contracts had dropped from a record $7.50 a bushel in late March to $3.68 earlier this month.
December crude oil fell 73 cents to $23.76 a barrel at the New York Mercantile Exchange after rising as high as $24.95.
Overseas, London's FTSE 100 index fell 15.3 points to 3,962.8. In Tokyo, the Nikkei 225 rose 233.78 points, or 1.12 percent, to 21,189.96.
